Before defining nominalism, you need to understand the problem it responds to, because without that context, the definition won't mean much. The problem is called the problem of universals, and it goes like this:

Look at a red apple, a red fire truck, and a red rose. You naturally call all three things "red." But why are you able to do that? What do those three things actually share?

Two possible answers exist:

Answer 1 — Realism: Those three objects all share a real, independently existing property called "redness." Redness is a universal — it exists as a genuine thing in the world, and each of those objects "has" or "participates in" it. When you call something red, you're pointing to this real, independent property.

Answer 2 — Nominalism: There is no such thing as "redness" floating around in the universe. The apple, the truck, and the rose don't share anything metaphysically real. What they share is only a name — the word "red." We humans noticed that these things look similar to us, so we invented a label for them. The label is useful and convenient, but it doesn't correspond to any independently existing thing in the world.

Nominalism is Answer 2.

Nominalism is the philosophical position that abstract concepts and general categories do not exist as real, independent things in the world. They are merely names — labels we attach to groups of similar individual things. Only concrete, particular, individual things truly exist.

The word to lock onto here is names. The nominalist sees words like "redness," "humanity," "beauty," "justice," and "the number five" as exactly that — names. Useful inventions of human language and thought. Not real things that exist independently out there in the world.

You have three pets: a golden retriever, a dalmatian, and a poodle. You call all three "dogs."

Now ask yourself: is there a thing called "dogness" — some essential property of being a dog — that exists independently of those three individual animals? Or did you simply observe that those three animals are similar enough to each other and decided to put them all under one convenient label: "dog"?

The nominalist says: there is no free-floating "dogness." The word "dog" is a label we invented for a group of similar creatures. Only the individual animals — this retriever, that dalmatian — are real. The category "dog" is just a name.

Now extend this logic to everything abstract. "Humanity," "triangularity," "the number five," "beauty," "justice" — none of these are real, independently existing things. They are names, concepts, and mental constructs. Only individual humans, individual triangles, individual beautiful objects are real.

The direct opposite of nominalism is realism (also called Platonic realism or universalism). Realists believe that abstract properties and categories — called universals — genuinely exist as real, independent things, separate from individual objects and separate from human minds.

Plato, the ancient Greek philosopher, is the most famous realist. He argued that for every category — beauty, justice, redness, triangularity — there exists a perfect, abstract "Form" in a non-physical realm. The beautiful things we see in the world are imperfect copies of the Form of Beauty. The triangles we draw are imperfect copies of the Form of Triangle.

Nominalism is, in large part, a rejection of exactly this kind of thinking. The nominalist says: there are no Forms, no abstract realm, no universals. There is only the physical world of individual things, and the names we attach to groups of them.

There is a third position sitting between realism and nominalism called conceptualism, and it's worth knowing because it helps sharpen what nominalism is saying.

Conceptualists say: universals exist, but only as mental concepts inside our minds — not as independently existing things out in the world. So "redness" is real as a concept in your head, but it doesn't exist independently of minds out there in nature.

Nominalism is stricter than this. For the nominalist, even calling a universal a real mental concept is saying too much. Universals are just names — linguistic labels — and nothing more. Nominalism locates universals entirely in language, not in the mind.

In practice, the line between nominalism and conceptualism gets debated, and some thinkers use the terms differently. But the key distinction is: nominalism says universals are just words or names; conceptualism says they are at least real ideas in the mind.

Nominalism is not a single rigid view — it's a family of related positions. Here are the main ones, in increasing sophistication:

Predicate Nominalism — The simplest version. A thing belongs to a category simply because a certain label or predicate applies to it. This apple is "red" just because the word "red" can correctly be applied to it. There's no deeper explanation needed. No shared property, no resemblance required — just the fact that the label fits.

Resemblance Nominalism — A more refined version. Things are grouped under the same name because they resemble each other. The apple, truck, and rose are all called "red" because they look similar to each other in a certain way. There is no universal "redness" — but the real resemblance between individual things is what justifies using the same name for all of them. For many people, this is the most intuitive version of nominalism, because it gives a reason for why we group things together beyond just "we invented a label."

Trope Nominalism — This version says that properties do exist, but they are not shared universals. Instead, each individual thing has its own unique, private instance of a property, called a trope. The redness of this specific apple is one individual instance of redness. The redness of that specific fire truck is a completely different individual instance of redness. These are two separate, particular things — not two objects sharing the same universal "redness." There are only individual things with individual private properties. The name "red" is what we use to group together all these individual redness-instances that resemble each other. No shared universal is needed.

Class Nominalism — A thing is red simply because it belongs to the class (or set) of red things. The class is just a collection. "Redness" is just a name for that collection. This avoids positing any universal property by replacing it with the notion of a set or class.
Why It Matters: Implications Across Different Fields

The debate between nominalism and realism isn't abstract puzzle-solving with no real-world stakes. It has significant consequences.

Mathematics — Do numbers exist as real things? A realist (called a Platonist in mathematics) says yes — the number 5 exists independently of human minds, just waiting to be discovered. A nominalist says no — "5" is a useful symbol and label we invented. There is no Platonic realm where numbers float around independently. This is one of the liveliest debates in the philosophy of mathematics today.

Science — When scientists classify animals into species, or matter into elements, are those categories real natural divisions in the world? Or are they useful labels humans invented? A realist says "tiger" as a species points to something genuinely real in nature. A nominalist says "tiger" is just a label humans invented to group similar-looking animals. There is no metaphysical glue binding all tigers together beyond our grouping of them.

Ethics and Morality — Is "justice" a real thing that exists in the world, waiting to be discovered? Moral realists say yes. Nominalists tend to say that "justice" is a concept humans invented — a name we give to certain arrangements and actions that we approve of. This deeply shapes how we think about whether moral truths are objective or constructed.

Religion and Theology — In medieval philosophy, debates about God's nature, the Trinity, and the soul were deeply tied to the nominalism vs. realism debate. This is one reason the debate was extraordinarily fierce in the Middle Ages — it wasn't just academic, it had religious consequences.

Language and Meaning — If category words like "dog," "red," or "justice" don't point to real things, then what exactly is language doing when we use such words? Nominalism forces us to think carefully about how words get their meaning and how communication works.

Plato (428–348 BC) — The great realist. Argued for the existence of abstract Forms as the most real things in existence.

Roscellinus (c. 1050–1125) — An early and radical nominalist who argued that universals are nothing more than puffs of air — mere sounds made by the human voice.

Peter Abelard (1079–1142) — A significant medieval thinker who argued against strong realism and held a position close to conceptualism. Often discussed alongside the nominalism debate.

William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) — The most famous and influential nominalist in history. He argued powerfully that universals exist only in the mind as mental concepts, and have no reality outside of it. He is also famous for Ockham's Razor — the principle that we should not multiply entities beyond what is necessary. His nominalism is a direct application of this: don't invent universals as extra, unnecessary entities when all you need are individual things and their names.

Nelson Goodman and W.V.O. Quine — Two major 20th-century analytic philosophers who defended forms of nominalism and made the debate central to modern philosophy.

"Nominalism means names don't matter or language is unimportant." Not at all. Nominalists take names very seriously — the entire point is that names are doing all the work. The claim is that categories are made of names and concepts, not that names are trivial.

"Nominalism means abstract concepts are fake or useless." No. The nominalist isn't saying "don't use the word 'redness' — it's meaningless." They're saying "redness" is a useful and legitimate name we apply to certain things, but there is no independently existing property called redness that the name "tracks." The name is useful; the claim is just about what kind of thing it refers to.

"Nominalism is obviously correct/obviously wrong." Neither. This is one of the oldest, most deeply contested debates in all of philosophy. Brilliant thinkers on both sides have been arguing about it for over two thousand years. Both positions have genuine strengths and face serious challenges.
The Summary, All in One Place

Nominalism is the philosophical position that only individual, concrete, particular things truly exist. Abstract concepts, general categories, and properties — like "redness," "justice," "humanity," or "the number five" — are not real, independently existing things in the world. They are merely names (labels) that we humans apply to groups of individual things that we perceive as similar. The word "red" does not point to a real universal property called redness existing independently in the universe — it is a useful label we invented for things that look similar to us.

Nominalism stands in direct opposition to realism, which holds that such universals are real and independent. It is also stricter than conceptualism, which says universals are at least real mental concepts, even if not things in the external world.

Within nominalism itself, the main variants differ on why we group things together: predicate nominalism says the label just applies; resemblance nominalism says the individual things genuinely resemble each other; trope nominalism says each thing has its own private property-instance; and class nominalism says membership in a set is all there is. All of them agree on the essential point: no universals, only particulars and names.
